\section[trīstitia, trīstitiae]{trīstitia, trīstitiae — sadness}

\label{lesson:LA-C490-tristitia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to leap for joy, then the Latin for pleasantness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: trīstitia, trīstitiae}
\textbf{trīstitia, trīstitiae} — \textquotedblleft{}sadness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Post mortem patris magna trīstitia domum tenet.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After the father's death great sadness fills the house.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, first declension, from \emph{trīstis} — sad.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{trīstitia} is built on \emph{trīstis} \textquotedblleft{}sad, gloomy\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-itia} (Lewis \& Short); EtymDB traces \emph{trīstis} to a Proto-Indo-European form meaning \textquotedblleft{}in a bad mood\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{trīstitia, trīstitiae}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{trīstitia, trīstitiae}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{trīstitia, trīstitiae}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to leap for joy, then the Latin for pleasantness, then say \emph{trīstitia, trīstitiae} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does trīstitia, trīstitiae mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Sadness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[maestitia, maestitiae]{maestitia, maestitiae — sorrow, dejection}

\label{lesson:LA-C490-maestitia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for pleasantness, then the Latin for sadness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: maestitia, maestitiae}
\textbf{maestitia, maestitiae} — \textquotedblleft{}sorrow, dejection\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Maestitia puellae ex oculīs eius appāret.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The girl's sorrow shows in her eyes.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, first declension, from \emph{maestus} — sad. A close partner of \emph{trīstitia}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{maestitia} is built on \emph{maestus} \textquotedblleft{}sad, sorrowful\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-itia} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maestitia, maestitiae}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{maestitia, maestitiae}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for pleasantness, then the Latin for sadness, then say \emph{maestitia, maestitiae} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[maereō, maerēre]{maereō, maerēre — to grieve, mourn}

\label{lesson:LA-C490-maereo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for sadness, then the Latin for sorrow.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: maereō, maerēre}
\textbf{maereō, maerēre} — \textquotedblleft{}to grieve, mourn\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Senex maeret, quod amīcus eius periit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The old man grieves because his friend has died.}
\end{quote}

\emph{maereō, maerēre, maeruī}; no supine in common use. Sadness that shows, as a mourner's does.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{maereō} is a native Latin verb; Lewis \& Short compares Greek \emph{misos} \textquotedblleft{}hatred\textquotedblright{} and Latin \emph{miser} \textquotedblleft{}wretched\textquotedblright{}, but EtymDB gives no parent, so the origin is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maereō, maerēre}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maereō, maerēre}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{maereō, maerēre}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for sadness, then the Latin for sorrow, then say \emph{maereō, maerēre} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does maereō, maerēre mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To grieve, mourn\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[maeror, maerōris]{maeror, maerōris — grief, mourning}

\label{lesson:LA-C490-maeror}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for sorrow, then the Latin for to grieve.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: maeror, maerōris}
\textbf{maeror, maerōris} — \textquotedblleft{}grief, mourning\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Maeror viduae magnus est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The widow's grief is great.}
\end{quote}

Masculine, third declension. Grief that shows, in tears and mourning clothes.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{maeror} is built on the verb \emph{maereō} \textquotedblleft{}to grieve\textquotedblright{} with the noun ending \emph{-or}, as \emph{dolor} is built on \emph{doleō} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maeror, maerōris}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{maeror, maerōris}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for sorrow, then the Latin for to grieve, then say \emph{maeror, maerōris} again

\section[lūctuōsus, lūctuōsa, lūctuōsum]{lūctuōsus, lūctuōsa, lūctuōsum — sorrowful, mournful}

\label{lesson:LA-C490-luctuosus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to grieve, then the Latin for grief.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lūctuōsus, lūctuōsa, lūctuōsum}
\textbf{lūctuōsus, lūctuōsa, lūctuōsum} — \textquotedblleft{}sorrowful, mournful\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ille diēs lūctuōsus omnibus cīvibus fuit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{That day was a sorrowful one for all the citizens.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{lūctus} — mourning. It can mean causing grief or feeling it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lūctuōsus} is built on \emph{lūctus} \textquotedblleft{}mourning\textquotedblright{}, the noun of \emph{lūgeō} \textquotedblleft{}to mourn\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{-ōsus} \textquotedblleft{}full of\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB derives it from \emph{lūctus}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{lūctuōsus, lūctuōsa, lūctuōsum}
